storm.summary_layperson: A batch of showers is tracking in from the southwest with a slight chance of embedded thunder, but there's essentially no atmospheric instability today, so don't expect anything beyond moderate rain — and the Sound isn't offering the cove any extra protection tonight since the water is actually running warmer than the air.
storm.local_effect_blurb: No marine-layer buffer in play — Sound water (65.3°F) is about 3°F warmer than the air, so there's no stabilizing gap to weaken incoming showers, and the trend confirms it stays that way (gap holds negative through 7 PM) rather than developing later in the window.
storm.detail_html:
KOKX radar shows scattered showers moving through western Long Island Sound, topping out around 36 dBZ and tracking fast at roughly 43 kt. NWS is calling for a 100% chance of rain this afternoon with only a slight chance of embedded thunder, and that fits the numbers — CAPE is reading 0 J/kg, essentially no instability, so this reads as a rain event rather than a convective or severe setup.

The nearest closing cell is 28 miles SW of the cove at 35 dBZ, closing at 32 kt, with a high-confidence radar-based ETA of 4:39 PM (window 4:28–4:51 PM). A second cell 41 miles SW is tracking similarly, ETA around 5:02 PM. A third cell just 5.7 miles NW is actually moving away and isn't a factor.

Neither of the cove's usual storm-weakening mechanisms is active tonight. Sound water (65.3°F) is running warmer than the air (62.6°F) — a -2.7°F gap — so there's no cold-water marine layer to stabilize the atmosphere, and the hour-by-hour trend shows that gap staying negative (down to -3.7°F by 7 PM) rather than building a buffer later. The sea breeze is also inactive. That means the cove should see this system at essentially the same intensity as surrounding inland towns — no local advantage tonight.

Separately, a Minor Coastal Flood Advisory is in effect starting 10 PM tonight through 2 PM tomorrow (NWS Upton) — tied to onshore/tidal timing rather than this storm, but worth knowing if you're near the water overnight.

What would change the call: a spike in CAPE as the system moves through, or a stronger cell developing within 25 miles at 45+ dBZ, would push this to high risk. Conversely, if the SW cells keep weakening the way they have been (35–36 dBZ, well below severe thresholds), risk should ease back toward low once this batch clears through the early evening.

arrival.blurb: Radar-tracked cell 28 mi SW closing at 32 kt; no marine-layer or sea-breeze buffer is active, so expect it at close to full strength around 4:40 PM.

wind.tactics_blurb: Steady NNE gradient breeze in the 12–15 kt range holding through the evening with no sea breeze involved — start mid-line and stay central, since this offshore-over-land direction tends to run puffier and shiftier than the models show, with no strong side advantage from the cove geography today.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
This is a gradient-only day — the air-water temperature difference is -2.7°F, well below the ~5°F threshold a sea breeze needs to build, and the sea-breeze station network confirms nothing is developing (0% of coastal stations reading southerly). With no thermal ingredient, this is Regime B-moderate regardless of the exact wind speed: forecast gradient wind runs 13–15 kt at NNE (022–029°) through the early window hours, squarely in the moderate bracket.

HRRR is forecasting NNE (~25°) while the broader western-Sound station average sits at ENE (68°, a 43° divergence, only 61% agreement) — but that zone average is dragged down by several near-calm APRS backyard stations reading 1–2 kt, where direction is essentially noise at that speed. RYC itself, the cove's own sensor and the best ground-truth read, is at NNE 22° — closely matching the HRRR call. Trust the NNE track.

NNE sits on the border between the cove geography table's "NE" row (clean offshore, laminar) and "N–NW" row (gusty, puffy, big oscillations) — and leaning this close to due north, expect the puffier character. That means gains and losses on shifts rather than a stable favored side — start mid-line, sail the shifts, and stay central rather than committing to one edge of the course.

Being gradient-only, this wind doesn't care about sunset (6:42 PM) — no collapse expected through the evening. HRRR's hourly model data cuts off at 7 PM (f05–f12 fetch failed); the 8–10 PM figures above are extrapolated from the standard B-moderate pattern (holds through sunset, may soften 1–2 kt after dark) rather than raw model output — treat them as directional guidance, lower confidence than the 5–7 PM numbers.

For the fleet: 12–15 kt sustained with gusts to 18–20 kt is solid full-crew breeze — comfortable, powered-up sailing without needing to depower smaller classes, though the puffy offshore character means helms should be anticipating gusts rather than getting caught flat.
